result.summary: Pausanias describes more offerings at Olympia: the bed of Hippodamia, the quoit of Iphitus, the ivory and gold table, and a relief of the gods. He tells of a dead soldier found in the roof of Hera's temple, the surviving pillar of Oenomaus' house, and the Philippeum with its statues of Philip's family.

scenes.title: Offerings and the games relief
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the bed, quoit and table, and the statues and carved scene of gods, including Pluto with his key.

scenes.title: Soldier in the temple roof
scenes.summary: Aristarchus tells of a wounded armoured man found dead in the roof of Hera's temple, a combatant in the old battle in the Altis. He was buried with his armour.
scenes.stakes: The wounded man was dying of his wounds in a hiding place.

scenes.title: Pillar of Œnomaus
scenes.summary: The one pillar saved from Œnomaus' burnt house stands near Zeus' temple, and a Roman senator's builders dig up ancient arms and bridles beside it.
scenes.stakes: The house of Œnomaus was destroyed by lightning.

scenes.title: Temple of the Mother, Philippeum
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Temple of the Mother and Philip's round house, built after Chaeronea and holding ivory and gold statues by Leochares.

notable_quotes.reason: The pillar's own inscribed voice, recording the survival of Œnomaus' house.

analysis.text: Relics link Olympia to myth and history, from Hippodamia and Œnomaus to Philip, making the sanctuary a living memory.
The Philippeum shows Macedonian rulers placing themselves in Greek sanctuaries after Chaeronea, and Roman-era emperors' statues show later powers doing likewise.

fun_facts.text: The Philippeum's foundations survive at Olympia and were excavated in the 19th century.

language_notes.text: The inscribed armistice runs in a circle around the quoit, not in straight lines. It is the sacred truce of Olympia, traditionally tied to Iphitus.
The sentence breaks off at a gap in the text; the name of Pasiteles' teacher is lost. The bracketed [73] is the translator's footnote marker.
Pluto is the god of the dead. Hades here means the underworld, not the god, and the key shows it is locked against return.
Interpreter of Antiquities translates the Greek exegetes, a local guide who explained the sanctuary's monuments and history to visitors.
The sham roof is a false ceiling, so the body lay hidden in the space between it and the tiled roof.
This refers to an earlier battle between Spartans (Lacedæmonians) and Eleans fought inside the sacred Altis, the precinct at Olympia.
Œnomaus was the legendary king of Pisa, father of Hippodamia, who killed her suitors in chariot races; his house stood at Olympia.
Elegiac lines are verse in couplets of a long hexameter line and a shorter pentameter, often used for inscriptions.
"Won the prize" means he was an Olympic victor; the statue and inscription would commemorate the win.
Altis was the sacred grove and precinct of Zeus at Olympia, containing the temples, altars and treasuries.
Chæronea (338 BC) was where Philip II of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes, ending the independence of the Greek cities.

context_notes.text: Iphitus was the traditional king of Elis who revived the Olympic games and the sacred truce. Hippodamia was the bride won by Pelops.
Æsculapius is the god of healing and Hygiea (Health) his daughter. Pluto rules the underworld, and Proserpine is his queen.
High buildings gave defenders a vantage point against attackers, so the Eleans used even temples as strongholds.
Arms and bridles found here would fit the old legend of Œnomaus' chariot racing and his slain suitors, which is probably why Pausanias mentions them.
Philip II ruled Macedon; Alexander is Alexander the Great, his son; Amyntas III was Philip's father.
Olympias was Philip's wife and Alexander's mother; Eurydice was Philip's mother. Leochares was a leading Athenian sculptor of the fourth century BC.

literary_notes.text: The key stands for the finality of death: the underworld is locked and none return.
Pausanias shows himself as a rational inquirer, offering a plausible explanation for why the body was so well preserved.
The lone pillar spared by the god's lightning stands for divine judgment on Œnomaus' house and for memory outlasting ruin.
The pillar speaks in the first person as a surviving witness, addressing the visitor directly and giving the relic a voice.
